title: Replication
scopeHtml: Scope: leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless, quorum math, replication lag fixes. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why replicate data
notes.html:
Replication means keeping copies of the same data on several machines. You do it for three reasons: survive a machine dying (availability), serve more reads (throughput), and put data near users (latency).

It does not help with data that is too big for one machine; that is sharding (next file). Every replication design answers one question: when a write happens, who accepts it, and who must confirm before we say "done"?

Worked example. A Postgres primary does 2,000 writes/s and 18,000 reads/s. One box handles about 20,000 total, so it is at the edge. Add 2 replicas for reads: primary keeps 2,000 writes, each replica serves 9,000 reads. Capacity is now roughly 3x for reads, 1x for writes.

Industry examples. Instagram and GitHub run Postgres/MySQL with many read replicas. Amazon Aurora keeps 6 copies of storage across 3 availability zones.

Everyday analogy. Photocopying an important document and keeping copies in different houses: a fire in one house does not lose it, but now you must keep all copies up to date.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying replication solves write scaling. It does not; every replica still applies every write.
  • Forgetting the cost: N copies means N times the storage and replication bandwidth.

notes.title: Leader-follower replication
notes.html:
One node (the leader, also called primary or master) accepts all writes. Followers (replicas) copy its changes and serve reads.

The leader writes each change to a log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog). Followers stream that log and replay it in the same order. Same order is the whole point: it guarantees followers converge to the same state.

Choices:

  • Synchronous: leader waits for the follower to confirm before acknowledging the client. No data loss, but one slow follower stalls writes.
  • Asynchronous: leader acknowledges immediately. Fast, but if the leader dies before the log reaches a follower, those writes are lost.
  • Semi-sync (the usual answer): wait for exactly one follower, the rest are async. Postgres: synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (r1, r2)'. MySQL has semi-sync plugin.

Worked example. Same-region follower round trip is about 1 ms; a cross-region one is about 80 ms. Fully sync across regions means every write costs at least 80 ms, so teams use sync in-region and async cross-region.

Failover. When the leader dies, promote the most up-to-date follower. Steps: detect (heartbeat timeout, for example 10 s), choose, repoint clients, make the old leader a follower when it returns. Danger: split brain, where the old leader comes back and still thinks it is the boss. Fix with fencing (kill the old node, lease/epoch numbers). Tools: Patroni for Postgres, Orchestrator for MySQL, Redis Sentinel.

Decision gravity. Choosing async is reversible by config but the data-loss window is accepted at design time. Choosing a single leader is chosen for simplicity (no write conflicts). It breaks when write volume exceeds one machine or when users are far from the leader. Switching later to multi-leader or sharding is a one-way door.

Industry examples. Postgres streaming replication, MySQL at Facebook/Uber (async with GTID), MongoDB replica sets (election among members using a Raft-like protocol), Redis replication (async by default).

Everyday analogy. One teacher writes on the board and students copy it into notebooks in the same order. Only the teacher writes, so notebooks never disagree, but if the teacher faints mid-sentence, someone has to take the chalk.

Common interview traps.

  • Promoting an async follower without admitting that acknowledged writes may be lost.
  • Ignoring split brain.
  • Saying "automatic failover is easy". Wrong detection (a slow network, not a dead node) causes needless failovers.

notes.title: Replication lag and how to hide it
notes.html:
Replication lag is the delay between a write on the leader and it appearing on a follower. Normally milliseconds; under load, a big transaction or a network blip, seconds or minutes.

Symptoms users see:

  • Read-your-writes violation: you post a comment, refresh, it is gone (the read hit a stale replica).
  • Monotonic read violation: you see a new post, refresh, it vanishes (second read hit a more lagged replica).
  • Causality violation: you see an answer before the question.

Fixes, cheapest first:

  1. Read from the leader right after a write (for example for 5 s, or for the user's own profile).
  2. Sticky replica per user (hash user id to a replica) so reads never go backwards in time.
  3. Track a position token: after a write, return the LSN/GTID; the next read goes only to a replica that has reached it (Postgres pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()).
  4. Route by lag: drop replicas lagging more than, say, 2 s from the pool.
-- Postgres: how far behind is this replica?
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS lag;

Worked example. A 2 GB bulk UPDATE on the leader replays serially on a replica (single-threaded in older MySQL), so lag jumps from 50 ms to 90 s while followers are busy. Metric: seconds_behind_master or replay_lag. Fix: batch updates in 10k-row chunks, use parallel replication.

Industry examples. Facebook's early architecture famously used a "recently wrote" cookie to pin users to the master for about 20 seconds. Many Rails apps use a similar primary-for-a-while trick.

Everyday analogy. You mail a letter and ask the post office if it was received; the clerk at a branch that has not updated yet says "no". Ask the original branch instead.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing "just use sync replication" without the latency and availability cost.
  • Not mentioning which guarantee you need (read-your-writes vs monotonic vs consistent prefix).

notes.title: Multi-leader replication
notes.html:
Several nodes accept writes, and each forwards its changes to the others. Typical use: one leader per region (Mumbai, Frankfurt, Virginia) so every user writes to a nearby node, and each region keeps working if the links between them break.

The price is write conflicts: two users edit the same row in different regions at the same moment, and both writes were accepted locally.

Conflict handling:

  • Avoid: route all writes for one record to the same region (home region of the user).
  • Last write wins (LWW): highest timestamp wins. Simple, silently loses data, and clocks drift.
  • Merge: keep both values (siblings) or use CRDTs (counters, sets that merge mathematically).
  • Custom resolver/app logic: ask the user, or apply business rules.

Real systems use all-to-all links (each leader sends to every other), which avoids one broken link stopping the flow but can reorder events.

Worked example. Two offices edit a calendar event title. Mumbai writes "Standup" at 10:00:00.100, Virginia writes "Sync" at 10:00:00.090 (clock skewed 20 ms behind). LWW keeps "Standup" even if Virginia's edit was actually later in real time. This is why important systems prefer version vectors over timestamps.

Decision gravity. Chosen when write latency across regions or offline operation matters more than simplicity. Alternatives: single leader plus follower reads, or sharding by region. It breaks when conflicts are frequent or data has invariants (account balance cannot go negative). Hard to undo, because data created with conflicts has already been merged lossily.

Industry examples. Google Docs style collaboration (operational transform/CRDT), CouchDB, MySQL Group Replication in multi-primary mode, Cassandra across datacenters (leaderless but similar effect), Active-active setups like AWS DynamoDB global tables (LWW by default).

Everyday analogy. Two people editing their own copy of a shared shopping list on separate phones; when they meet, the lists must be merged and someone bought milk twice.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing multi-leader just for "high availability" when a single leader with failover suffices.
  • Using auto-increment ids, unique constraints or counters across leaders without handling conflicts.

notes.title: Leaderless replication and quorum math
notes.html:
No leader: the client (or a coordinator) sends each write to several replicas and each read to several replicas, and compares answers. This is the Dynamo design (Amazon Dynamo paper, then Cassandra, Riak, ScyllaDB).

Parameters: N replicas hold each key, W must acknowledge a write, R must answer a read.

Rule: if W + R > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (assuming no concurrent writes and no sloppy quorum).

N W R Property
3 2 2 Balanced, tolerates 1 node down for both
3 3 1 Fast reads, writes fail if any node down
3 1 3 Fast writes, reads slow
3 1 1 W+R=2, not greater than 3, can read stale, max availability

Worked example. N=3, W=2, R=2. Write v2 reaches A and B; C is down. A read asks B and C: B returns v2, C returns v1 (old). The coordinator picks the newer version by timestamp/version and does a read repair, writing v2 to C. Background anti-entropy using Merkle trees repairs keys nobody reads.

Other tools:

  • Hinted handoff: if C is down, another node stores the write with a hint and gives it to C when it returns.
  • Sloppy quorum: accept writes on any N healthy nodes even if not the home nodes, trading consistency for availability. W+R>N no longer guarantees fresh reads.
  • Cassandra consistency levels: ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL. Typical production: LOCAL_QUORUM for both reads and writes with RF=3 per datacenter.
-- cqlsh
CONSISTENCY LOCAL_QUORUM;
INSERT INTO orders (id, status) VALUES (42, 'PAID');

Edge cases where quorum still gives stale reads. Concurrent write and read, a write that failed partway (applied on some nodes but reported failure), a node restored from stale backup, clock skew with LWW.

Decision gravity. Chosen for availability and no failover pause (no leader to elect). Alternative: consensus-based (Raft in etcd, Spanner), which gives strong consistency at higher latency. It breaks for workloads needing transactions or strict ordering. Switching later is a one-way door because the data model (wide rows, no joins) changes.

Industry examples. Amazon DynamoDB (originally Dynamo), Apple runs huge Cassandra clusters (reported over 100k nodes), Discord used Cassandra for messages then moved to ScyllaDB, Netflix uses Cassandra for viewing history.

Everyday analogy. A decision needs signatures from 2 of 3 managers; any 2 managers always share at least one person who knows the latest decision.

Common interview traps.

  • Stating W+R>N guarantees strong consistency. It does not under sloppy quorum or concurrent writes.
  • Mixing up N (copies) with the cluster size.
  • Forgetting that a quorum write needs W replicas up; with N=3, W=3 is less available than a single leader.

notes.title: Choosing a replication style
notes.html:
Simple decision flow:

  1. Need transactions, joins, strict consistency, one region? Single leader, semi-sync follower in the same region, async elsewhere.
  2. Users spread over continents and writes must be local, conflicts tolerable? Multi-leader with home-region routing.
  3. Massive write volume, always-on, simple key-value access, eventual consistency OK? Leaderless with quorums.
  4. Need strong consistency and automatic failover across zones? Consensus replication (Raft/Paxos: etcd, CockroachDB, Spanner, MongoDB majority writes).

Worked example. A payments ledger: leader-follower with sync replica in another AZ (RPO=0), ROUTE reads for balances to leader. A chat history store: Cassandra RF=3, LOCAL_QUORUM, since a message appearing a few ms late is fine.

Everyday analogy. One editor-in-chief (leader), several regional editors (multi-leader), or a committee voting (quorum).

Common interview traps.

  • Picking a style without stating the consistency requirement and RPO/RTO targets.
  • Forgetting cross-region latency numbers (Mumbai to Virginia about 200 ms RTT).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Replication = copies for availability, read throughput and latency. It does not scale writes.
  • Leader-follower: one writer, ordered log; sync vs async vs semi-sync trades latency for data-loss risk. Beware split brain on failover.
  • Replication lag causes stale reads: fix with read-your-writes (pin to leader), monotonic reads (sticky replica), LSN tokens, lag-based routing.
  • Multi-leader: local writes everywhere, but conflicts; prefer avoiding them, else merge or LWW (lossy).
  • Leaderless: N, W, R; W+R>N gives overlap but not magic; read repair, hinted handoff, anti-entropy.
  • Pick by consistency need, geography and write volume; leader changes are one-way doors.
